extracted.intended_audience: educated general reading public interested in manners, satire, and moral criticism (early-18th-century periodical readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, didactic/satirical prose pieces about manners, character, and societal oddities that use anecdote and moral reflection to amuse and instruct. The page shows how to choose comic targets, deploy concrete detail, and close with moral or corrective judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative justice / satisfying retribution
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Mind of Man is naturally a Lover of Justice, and when we read a Story wherein a Criminal is overtaken, in whom there is no Quality which is the Object of Pity, the Soul enjoys a certain Revenge for the Offence done to its Nature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story gains emotional satisfaction when a villain who has no redeeming/piteous qualities is finally punished; exemplified by the Rhynsault tale where the governor's crimes are exposed and punished. Anti-pattern: failing to give the reader a sense of just recompense reduces the moral/affective payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by precise mannerisms and “airs”
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed listing of coquettes' 'airs'—a dancing walk, an early entrance with a run, a pretty shiver, carrying the fan between both hands, falling into the lowest seat so the hoop'd petticoats fall 'with a lucky Decency,' coming into company out of breath, staring until a man is 'got' then becoming short-sighted, swinging on ropes with playful shrieks, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, recognizable physical gestures and habitual little tricks to make comic female character-types vivid and believable. Such particular actions (entrances, posture, facial tricks, small theatricalities) are effective comic material because they let readers ‘see’ the character. Anti-pattern: vagueness or abstraction; absence of such details makes satire limp or unconvincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anecdote and confrontation to expose vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Long anecdotal telling (e.g., Rhynsault's abuse of power and Sapphira's formal complaint to the Duke) culminating in a public confrontation and moral resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame vice in a concrete narrative that leads to a decisive public reckoning (confrontation, confession, punishment) — this both entertains and enforces the essay's moral point. The anecdote should include specific actions and a denouement that illustrates the lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good recommendation letters: modesty, restraint, and strong grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: From Horace (translation): a recommender 'has a Slowness to ask a Favour, a strong Reason for being unable to deny his good Word any longer, and that it is a Service to the Person to whom he recommends, to comply with what is asked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper letter of recommendation should show modesty in asking the favour, provide compelling reasons for making the recommendation (not merely convenience), and demonstrate that granting the request is actually in the recipient's interest. Anti-patterns: casual blanket praise, using recommendations as mere charity or to offload an unwanted person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and prudence in giving character references
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of social tendency to pass 'worthless Creatures' by polite testimonials and of professional 'undertakers' who supply defective recommendations; anecdote of Jack Toper giving a truthful, tailored account emphasizing fit rather than flattering universal praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not give blanket or false praise; instead, tailor references honestly to the needs and temperament of the prospective employer. If a candidate has faults (e.g., too orderly for a tavern life), state them honestly so the match succeeds. Anti-pattern: perfunctory or charitable references that harm third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent piety with cheerfulness rather than gloom
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is no unpleasant matter ... that every one that would be thought religious, to throw as much Sanctity as possible into his Face, and in particular to abstain from all Appearances of Mirth and Pleasantry...’ and the counter-argument: 'The true Spirit of Religion cheers, as well as composes the Soul; it banishes indeed all Levity of Behaviour, all vicious and dissolute Mirth, but in exchange fills the Mind with a perpetual Serenity, uninterrupted Chearfulness...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid portraying religious devotion as morose, unsociable melancholy. Good moral/religious character in an essay should show cheerfulness, serenity, and social affability while excluding vice and levity — humor and piety are compatible when regulated by virtue. Anti-pattern: using religiosity as an excuse for sourness and social discouragement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy by inverted age-appropriate behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that it is 'a monstrous want of Reflection' when aged persons put on the outward Pomp and Lustre of youth (e.g., an older man dressed in extravagant youth's fashion while his son is deprived of innocent diversions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire is effective when it exposes absurdity created by people behaving in ways contrary to social/chronological expectations (old men adopting youth's vanities). Use contrast between expected role and actual behaviour to generate ridicule and moral point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid simile and theatrical comparison for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples like comparing a woman's falling into a chair to an actress falling dead in a tragedy, or observing that certain airs are performed 'as well as you may have seen an Actress fall down dead in a Tragedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ striking, theatrical similes to heighten comic description and make the scene instantly imaginable. Metaphor and comparison that draw on familiar stage images sharpen satire and produce a laugh by exposing artifice. Anti-pattern: overextended or obscure figurative language that blunts immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social observation of fashions and small customs as comic material
rubrics_metrics.description: Across pieces, minuteness about popular behaviours (recommendation conventions, domestic service, coquettish airs, swinging pastimes, oddities of dress) provides the basis for gentle moral correction and entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and report precise, local details of manners and fashions; these small particulars create recognisable targets for satire and allow the essayist to generalize a social lesson. Anti-pattern: general moralizing without anchoring in observable, amusing particulars.
